fact: Requirements discovery is the process and techniques used by systems analysts to identify and extract system PROBLEMS and solution requirements from the user community, working together with users
A PROBLEM is an undesirable situation that prevents the organisation from fully achieving its mission, vision, goals and objectives

Requirements discovery requires analytical, communication and interpersonal skills; analysts must listen carefully, ask the right questions, resolve conflicting requirements, and validate findings with stakeholders to ensure accuracy and completeness
The process of requirements discovery consists of FOUR activities: problem discovery and analysis, requirements discovery, documenting and analysing requirements, and requirements management
Two types of requirements are identified during discovery: FUNCTIONAL and NON-FUNCTIONAL

Common fact-gathering techniques used during requirements discovery include interviews, questionnaires, workplace user observation, document analysis, facilitated workshops or Joint Application Development sessions, and sometimes prototyping to help users visualise features

System requirements are statements that specify what an information system should do and the conditions under which it must operate; they define expected functions, behaviour and constraints and serve as a formal agreement between stakeholders and the development team

In simple terms, system requirements are what the information system must DO, which are functional requirements, or what it must HAVE, which are non-functional requirements; they are also called business requirements
System requirements are developed during the system ANALYSIS phase and provide the basis for system design, implementation, testing and evaluation

The SIX results of incorrect requirements are: the system may cost more than projected; it may be delivered later than promised; it may not meet users' expectations, causing them not to use it; the costs of maintaining and enhancing it in production may be excessively high; it may be unreliable, prone to errors and downtime; and the reputation of the IT staff is tarnished because any failure is perceived as the team's mistake

FACT-FINDING is the formal process of using research, meetings, interviews, questionnaires, sampling and other techniques to collect information about system problems, requirements and preferences; it is also called information gathering or data collection
Fact-finding brings analysts into contact with sensitive information such as company plans, employee salaries or medical history, and customer credit card or social security information
The analyst's ethical behaviour has two duties: systems analysts must NOT MISUSE that information, and must PROTECT it from people who would misuse it

Breaching fact-finding ethics means the analyst loses respect, credibility and confidence of users and management, impairing the ability to do the job; the organisation and analyst could have legal liability; and the analyst could lose a job

A Requirements Definition Document is a formal document that communicates the requirements of a proposed system to key stakeholders and serves as a CONTRACT for the system's project; it gives a high-level description of system functions and constraints, written in business language

Draft requirements are documented with three tools: USE CASES, which describe how actors interact with the system to achieve goals and focus on what the system does from the user's perspective; DECISION TABLES, which represent complex business rules by listing all conditions and corresponding actions in a table; and REQUIREMENTS TABLES, which organise requirements with an ID, description, type, source, priority and status
The requirements definition document is also referred to as the requirements definition report, requirements statement, requirements specification, or functional specifications

There are SEVEN fact-finding techniques: sampling of existing documentation, forms and databases; research and site visits; observation of the work environment; questionnaires; interviews; prototyping; and joint requirements planning

Sampling of existing documentation reviews the organisation chart, memos and documents describing the problem, standard operating procedures, completed forms, manual and computerised screens and reports, samples of databases, and flowcharts and other system documentation

Sampling existing documents gives insight into current business processes, business rules and information requirements, and helps identify redundancies and inconsistencies in processes and recordkeeping as well as data quality issues

OBSERVATION is a technique in which the analyst either participates in or observes a person performing activities to learn about the system; it uncovers informal procedures, workarounds, bottlenecks and inefficiencies that users may not mention during interviews, and gives first-hand understanding of how work is done

The nine observation guidelines are: determine the who, what, where, when, why and how of the observation; obtain permission from appropriate supervisors or managers; inform those who will be observed of the purpose; keep a low profile; take notes during or immediately following the observation; review observation notes with appropriate individuals; do not interrupt the individuals at work; do not focus heavily on trivial activities; and do not make assumptions
A QUESTIONNAIRE is a special-purpose document that allows the analyst to collect information and opinions from respondents, useful when information is needed from many people quickly and at low cost

A FREE-FORMAT questionnaire offers the respondent greater latitude in the answer, with the answer recorded in the space provided; a FIXED-FORMAT questionnaire requires selecting an answer from predefined responses, and its types include multiple-choice, rating, and ranking questions

An INTERVIEW is a technique whereby analysts collect information from individuals through face-to-face interaction; it can be used to find facts, verify facts, clarify facts, generate enthusiasm, get the end-user involved, identify requirements, and solicit ideas and opinions

An UNSTRUCTURED interview is conducted with only a general goal or subject in mind and with few if any specific questions, the interviewer counting on the interviewee to provide a framework and direct the conversation

A STRUCTURED interview is one in which the interviewer has a specific set of questions to ask; within it an OPEN-ENDED question allows the interviewee to respond in any way that seems appropriate, while a CLOSED-ENDED question restricts answers to specific choices or short direct responses

The interview procedure has five stages: define the objective of the interview, select interviewees, prepare for the interview using an interview guide which is a checklist of specific questions, conduct the interview, and follow up on the interview

Guidelines for communicating during an interview: approach the session with a positive attitude, set the other person at ease, let them know you are listening, ask questions, do not assume anything, take notes, and attend to body language, which is the non-verbal information we communicate, including facial disclosure, eye contact and posture

Following up on the interview means validating the documented responses with the interviewee or relevant stakeholders to ensure correctness and avoid misunderstandings, which enhances the reliability of the gathered information

DISCOVERY PROTOTYPING is the act of building a small-scale, representative or working model of the users' requirements to discover or verify those requirements; it is particularly useful when requirements are unclear or when user interface design is critical to system success

JOINT REQUIREMENTS PLANNING is a process whereby highly structured group meetings are conducted for the purpose of analysing problems and defining requirements; JRP is a SUBSET of the more comprehensive Joint Application Development technique, which encompasses the entire systems development process
JRP participants are the sponsor, the facilitator, users and managers, scribes who take notes, and IT staff

The three steps to plan a JRP session are selecting a location, away from the workplace when possible and requiring several rooms equipped with tables, chairs, whiteboard, overhead projectors and computer equipment; selecting the participants, each released from regular duties; and preparing the agenda, with briefing documentation distributed before each session

Guidelines for a successful JRP session: do not unreasonably deviate from the agenda; stay on schedule; ensure the scribe can take notes; avoid technical jargon; apply conflict resolution skills; allow ample breaks; encourage group consensus; encourage user and management participation without allowing individuals to dominate; and make sure attendees abide by the established ground rules

BRAINSTORMING is a technique for generating ideas by encouraging participants to offer as many ideas as possible in a short period of time, WITHOUT ANY ANALYSIS until all the ideas have been exhausted; one goal of a JRP session is to generate possible solutions to a problem, and brainstorming is the common approach used

Brainstorming guidelines: isolate the appropriate people free from distractions; make sure everyone understands the purpose; appoint one person to record ideas; remind everyone of the rules; within a specified period team members call out ideas as fast as they think of them; only after the group has run out of ideas and all are recorded should they be analysed and evaluated; then refine, combine and improve the ideas generated

The three benefits of JRP are that it actively involves users and management in the project, encouraging them to take ownership; it reduces the amount of time required to develop systems; and when JRP incorporates prototyping as a means for confirming requirements and obtaining design approvals, the benefits of prototyping are realised
